lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | May 2023 - Jul 2024
- Rebuilt the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards around per-sensor error budgets, cutting mean time to detect incidents from 40 to 12 minutes.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases and adds automated regression checks that shortened release cycles to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation

items.says: Experience is not listed newest-first.
items.because: The older Eastern Robotics role appears above the newer Mobility Systems role, making the chronology harder to scan.

items.says: The dashboard change alone does not establish that it caused mean time to detect to fall from 40 to 12 minutes.
items.because: Detection time also depends on alerting and responders, and the line gives no measurement basis.

items.says: The bullet shifts from past tense to present tense in a role that ended in July 2024.
items.because: “Maintained” describes completed work, but “adds” sounds like a current responsibility.

items.says: The line does not establish that the automated regression checks shortened release cycles to three days.
items.because: It does not show that manual testing or regression-related rework was the bottleneck or that the checks drove the change.

items.says: “Shortened release cycles to 3 days” gives an endpoint but no starting duration.
items.because: A reader cannot tell how large the improvement was without the prior cycle time.

items.says: The line does not establish that the listed changes removed the nightly backlogs.
items.because: An event queue will not necessarily clear a backlog if downstream processing capacity is the bottleneck.

items.says: The bullet obscures which change caused the backlog result and what you owned.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the migration, logging rewrite, onboarding, or on-call work produced the improvement.

items.says: The backlog result comes after a long list of actions and responsibilities.
items.because: A scanning reader must get through the other details before reaching the result.

items.says: “Cutting the pending-case backlog 68%” attributes the entire reduction to the triage branch based only on timing after launch.
items.because: Incoming case volume, staffing, or other process changes could also have changed the backlog.

items.says: “Single-request edge inference” conflicts with crediting dynamic batching for the latency reduction.
items.because: A lone request cannot benefit from being batched with other requests, and batching wait can add latency.

items.says: The listed reward components do not establish the claimed 5% end-to-end latency reduction.
items.because: They could affect latency indirectly, but the line gives no comparable end-to-end measurement.

items.says: The 5% latency change lacks a workload and baseline latency.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what system or evaluation the improvement describes.

items.says: The method-first opening leaves the actor responsible for the latency reduction unclear.
items.because: A reader has to infer who or what produced the result.

items.says: One scored rollout per prompt cannot provide the within-prompt comparisons used by standard GRPO.
items.because: Standard GRPO estimates relative advantages from multiple rollouts for the same prompt.

items.says: “So each update used exactly one scored trajectory” repeats the one-rollout detail without adding a distinct result.
items.because: The preceding phrase already says training sampled one rollout per prompt.

items.says: The opening adoption claim is generic beside the concrete latency and task-completion results.
items.because: It names no specific outcome and draws attention away from the quantified results.

items.says: The move from 900 ms to 600 ms is a 33.3% reduction, not a 50% reduction.
items.because: The decrease is 300 ms out of the 900 ms starting value.

items.says: The change from 71% to 83% is 12 percentage points, not a 12% increase.
items.because: Relative to the 71% starting rate, the increase is about 16.9%.

items.says: The ongoing benchmark adoption result comes after a long clause.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the adoption only after the metric details.

items.says: The Kendall correlation does not identify what was correlated with what.
items.because: Without the reference measure or ranking, a reader cannot tell what the correlation demonstrates.

items.says: The correlation result is delayed behind methodological detail.
items.because: Foregrounding the correlation would make the main finding easier to notice.

items.says: The upstream fixes appear after the instrumentation detail.
items.because: Placing the outcome nearer the start would help a scanning reader find it.
